content: Diastasis recti is a medical condition characterized by the separation of the rectus abdominis muscle into two distinct halves, the right and left sides. Normally, these two sides are connected at the midline by a fibrous structure called the linea alba. This condition primarily affects two groups of individuals: newborns and pregnant women. In newborns, the rectus abdominis muscle may not be fully developed or fused at the midline, leading to diastasis recti. This is more frequently observed in premature infants and African American newborns. In pregnant or postpartum women, the separation occurs due to the stretching of the rectus abdominis muscle caused by the expanding uterus. Women who have had multiple pregnancies are at a higher risk because of repeated episodes of muscle stretching. During pregnancy, the uterus may sometimes protrude through the abdominal wall, creating a visible bulge beneath the skin. Clinically, diastasis recti presents as a ridge or bulge running along the midline of the abdomen, extending from the xiphoid process (the lower part of the sternum) to the umbilicus (belly button). When the abdominal muscles are relaxed, the ridge may disappear. On physical examination, the medial edges of the separated muscle halves can often be palpated when the abdominal wall is relaxed. The diagnosis of diastasis recti is typically made through a physical examination. In cases where a ventral hernia is suspected, ultrasound imaging can be used to rule out this condition. Treatment is generally not required for pregnant women while they are still carrying their child. However, in rare cases, complications such as the development of an umbilical or ventral hernia may occur in children. These hernias can be surgically corrected if necessary.
